scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Boria is a form of Malay theatre of Indian origin that became established in Penang, Malaysia.
It was first mentioned by H.T. Haughton in 1897, who reported that it was brought to Penang in 1845 by Muslim soldiers of the 21st Madras Regiment.
Initially performed to celebrate the annual Shiite festival, the Mourning of Muharram, it evolved significantly over the following decades.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Boria was originally played to celebrate the annual Shiite festival of the Mourning of Muharram.
Through adaptive cultural processes, it became a central theatre tradition of the Malay community in Penang.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music of Boria features the violin as the consistent main melodic instrument.
The percussion ensemble includes various Western, Malay, or Indian drums as well as Chinese cymbals.
Listen for the violin, Western drums, Malay drums, Indian drums.

A melodic violin line leads the performance, supported by rhythmic accompaniment from Western, Malay, or Indian drums and Chinese cymbals. The vocal structure features alternating solo lines and choral responses set to Western-influenced popular dance rhythms.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes and comic improvisations in Boria revolve around varying theatrical themes.
These thematic portrayals range from Arab warriors and European traders to Chinese shopkeepers, with performers costumed accordingly for stage presentation.

scenes.title: The people
narration: R.J. Wilkinson documented a distinction between the original Boria of Madras and the evolved Boria of Penang in 1910, noting that the Penang form had developed a distinct regional character.

Boria originated among the Muslim soldiers of the 21st Madras Regiment and migrated to Penang, where it transitioned from a Shiite religious festival observance into a localized Malay song-dance theatre form.

Instruments: violin, Western drums, Malay drums, Indian drums, Chinese cymbals. Vocal style: juxtaposition of choral and solo parts. Form: short comic sketches followed by song-dance routine. Mood: theatrical, comic, lively. It should sound like this: A melodic violin line leads the performance, supported by rhythmic accompaniment from Western, Malay, or Indian drums and Chinese cymbals. The vocal structure features alternating solo lines and choral responses set to Western-influenced popular dance rhythms. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
